The reservoir at dawn

By Immy Fisher · 6 min read

The water sits so still before sunrise that the far ridge appears twice, once in rock and once in a softer grey below it. Ducks cut the reflection into moving wedges and it knits itself back together behind them, slower each time as the air warms.

By seven the wind arrives through the gap in the hills and the mirror is gone for the day, traded for a million small facets that never hold a shape long enough to name. The herons give up on stealth and just wade.

Why the level drops in August

Two things pull the surface down at once: the city drawing harder in the heat, and a month with almost no rain to top it back up. The old high-water line shows as a pale band on the concrete, a foot above where the lake actually is.

  • Inflow from the two feeder streams roughly halves between June and September.
  • Evaporation alone can take a centimetre off the whole reservoir on a hot, dry day.
